title: The Burned Scroll
overview: Jeremiah 36 recounts a pivotal moment in the prophet Jeremiah’s ministry during the reign of King Jehoiakim of Judah. God commands Jeremiah to write down all His words of judgment against Israel, Judah, and the nations. Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe, reads the scroll publicly, but the message provokes fear and rejection among the officials and the king. Jehoiakim burns the scroll in defiance, yet God instructs Jeremiah to write the words again with added warnings. This chapter highlights the tension between divine truth and human rebellion, showcasing God’s sovereignty and the prophet’s obedience amid hostility. It underscores the seriousness of rejecting God’s word and the certainty of judgment for persistent disobedience.
structure:
**Verses 1-7: Divine Command and Purpose.** God instructs Jeremiah to write all His words of judgment to provoke repentance in Judah and Israel, hoping they will turn from evil and receive forgiveness.

**Verses 8-18: Public Reading and Official Reaction.** Baruch reads the scroll publicly on a fast day; officials hear the words and fearfully report them to the king, questioning Baruch about the scroll’s origin and advising Jeremiah and Baruch to hide.

**Verses 19-26: The King’s Defiance.** The scroll is brought before King Jehoiakim, who listens as Jehudi reads it, then cuts and burns the scroll in the fire, showing blatant rejection of God’s message despite intercession from his officials.

**Verses 27-32: Divine Response and Renewal of the Scroll.** God commands Jeremiah to write another scroll with the original words plus additional warnings against Jehoiakim’s rebellion and foretells his judgment, emphasizing God’s unyielding authority.

keyVerses.text: It may be that the house of Judah will hear all the evil which I purpose to do unto them; that they may return every man from his evil way; that I may forgive their iniquity and their sin.
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals God's merciful intent behind the prophetic warnings: to bring Judah to repentance and forgiveness. It highlights the purpose of prophecy as a call to change, not merely judgment.

keyVerses.text: And it came to pass, that when Jehudi had read three or four leaves, he cut it with the penknife, and cast it into the fire that was on the hearth, until all the roll was consumed in the fire that was on the hearth.
keyVerses.significance: This dramatic act by King Jehoiakim symbolizes the rejection of God's word and authority. It serves as a powerful illustration of human rebellion against divine truth and the consequences of such defiance.

keyVerses.text: And thou shalt say to Jehoiakim king of Judah, Thus saith the LORD; Thou hast burned this roll, saying, Why hast thou written therein, saying, The king of Babylon shall certainly come and destroy this land, and shall cause to cease from thence man and beast?
keyVerses.significance: This verse records God's direct confrontation with Jehoiakim’s contempt for the prophecy, affirming the certainty of Babylonian judgment despite the king’s denial and destruction of the scroll.

keyVerses.text: And I will punish him and his seed and his servants for their iniquity; and I will bring upon them, and upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and upon the men of Judah, all the evil that I have pronounced against them; but they hearkened not.
keyVerses.significance: This verse underscores the certainty of divine judgment on Jehoiakim and Judah due to their persistent disobedience, emphasizing the consequences of ignoring God's warnings.

characters.name: Jeremiah
characters.description: The prophet of God who receives the divine command to write down God's words of judgment. He faithfully obeys despite personal risk and the king’s hostility.

characters.name: Baruch
characters.description: Jeremiah’s scribe who writes the scroll as dictated and publicly reads it. He plays a crucial role in communicating God's message to the people and officials.

characters.name: Jehoiakim
characters.description: King of Judah who violently rejects God's word by burning the scroll. His actions reveal his rebellion and unwillingness to repent, leading to divine judgment.

characters.name: God
characters.description: The sovereign Lord who commands Jeremiah to write His words, seeks repentance from Judah, pronounces judgment, and ensures His message is preserved despite opposition.

themes.description: Jeremiah and Baruch’s faithful transcription and public reading of God's message contrast sharply with Jehoiakim’s rejection, highlighting the call to obey God’s revealed truth.
God’s warnings aim to provoke repentance and forgiveness, yet persistent disobedience results in judgment, reflecting the balance of God’s justice and grace.
The scroll represents God’s authoritative word. Jehoiakim’s attempt to destroy it illustrates human resistance to divine authority, but God’s command to rewrite it affirms Scripture’s enduring power.
Jeremiah’s role as God’s messenger demonstrates the prophet’s duty to faithfully proclaim God’s word regardless of opposition or personal danger.

historicalContext: This chapter is set during the reign of Jehoiakim (c. 609–598 BC), a period of political instability in Judah under increasing Babylonian pressure. Jerusalem was the religious and political center, with the temple as the focal point of worship and public life. Fasting days were significant communal religious observances. The scribal culture was well established, with officials like Baruch and Gemariah serving important roles in recording and preserving texts. Jehoiakim’s reign was marked by rebellion against Babylon, and his rejection of Jeremiah’s prophecy reflects the broader tension between divine sovereignty and human kingship in a time of national crisis.

theologicalInterpretations.description: This perspective emphasizes God’s sovereign control over history and the certainty of judgment for unrepentant sinners. Jeremiah’s obedience and the preservation of God’s word despite opposition underscore the doctrine of Scripture’s divine inspiration and authority.

Dispensationalists see the chapter as illustrating God’s prophetic program and the consequences of rejecting His revealed will. The burning of the scroll typifies human resistance to God’s plans, but God’s faithfulness ensures His promises and warnings are fulfilled.

Early church interpreters often viewed Jeremiah’s scroll as a type of the Scriptures and Christ’s word, with Jehoiakim’s burning symbolizing rejection of divine truth. The call to repentance and the promise of judgment were seen as timeless warnings for the church.

crossReferences.connection: Isaiah’s writing of a prophetic message on a tablet parallels Jeremiah’s writing on a scroll, emphasizing the importance of preserving God’s word.
Affirms the divine inspiration and authority of Scripture, underscoring why the burning of Jeremiah’s scroll was a serious offense.
The theme of judgment for rejecting God’s word is echoed in the final judgment scene where deeds are judged according to the books.
Describes God’s word as a lamp to the feet, highlighting the necessity of heeding Scripture rather than rejecting it as Jehoiakim did.
Encourages trust and obedience to God’s guidance, contrasting with Jehoiakim’s rebellion against God’s revealed will.

application: Commit to faithfully reading and obeying God’s Word, even when it challenges or convicts you.
Recognize the seriousness of rejecting God’s truth and the consequences of persistent disobedience.
Encourage others to hear and respond to God’s warnings with repentance and humility.
Trust in God’s sovereignty to preserve His Word despite opposition or persecution.
Pray for courage and wisdom to proclaim God’s truth faithfully in difficult circumstances.
conclusion: Jeremiah 36 powerfully illustrates the clash between divine truth and human rebellion. Through Jeremiah and Baruch’s obedience and Jehoiakim’s defiance, the chapter reveals the enduring authority of God’s Word and the urgent call to repentance. It warns believers today of the dangers of rejecting Scripture and encourages steadfast faithfulness in proclaiming and living out God’s message. The chapter’s themes of judgment, mercy, and prophetic witness remain vital for understanding God’s dealings with His people and the necessity of submission to His sovereign will.
timeline: c. 605 BC - Early reign of Jehoiakim, shortly after Babylon’s rise to dominance in the Near East

definitions.definition: A scroll made of parchment or papyrus on which writings were recorded, commonly used for books in ancient times.
A designated day of abstaining from food and sometimes drink, observed for repentance, mourning, or seeking God’s favor.
A trained official who copied documents, recorded events, and preserved texts, often serving prophets and kings.
A small knife used for cutting or trimming, here used by Jehudi to cut the scroll before burning it.

outline.heading: God’s Command to Write the Prophecy
outline.description: God instructs Jeremiah to write down all His words of judgment against Israel and Judah, hoping the people will repent and be forgiven.

outline.heading: Public Reading of the Scroll
outline.description: Baruch reads the scroll publicly on a fast day; officials hear the words, fear the message, and report it to the king, advising Jeremiah and Baruch to hide.

outline.heading: King Jehoiakim’s Rejection
outline.description: Jehoiakim listens to the scroll but then burns it in defiance, refusing to heed the warnings despite intercession from his officials.

outline.heading: God’s Command to Rewrite the Scroll
outline.description: God commands Jeremiah to write another scroll with the original words plus additional warnings, reaffirming the certainty of judgment on Jehoiakim and Judah.
